READING PASSAGE 2

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

How to be Happy

Some recent developments in the science of happiness

A A psychiatrist Tony Fernando was walking down the street when he saw a group of young homeless men sitting on the footpath. As Fernando handed out gifts of food, he tried to video the men's reactions in his mind, recording how their gratitude lifted him in return. 'I felt warm, content, meaningful,' he says. Fernando believes the brain can be trained to make us happy and that his ‘video method' is one way to achieve this. In fact, a growing body of scientific research internationally is showing how we can learn happiness in the same way we can learn to play the piano. In the soft tissue that forms the brain, there are approximately ten trillion synapses connecting roughly a hundred billion neurons. Active synapses become more sensitive; less active synapses die, but new ones grow quickly. This is relatively new thinking – just 30 years ago, neuroscientists believed that adult brain cells couldn't regenerate. One of the pioneers in this field is University of Wisconsin professor Richard Davidson. He studied Buddhist monks using brain scans in his research facility, and found that those trained in meditation had higher levels of activity in the left prefrontal cortex – the area associated with happiness. Davidson believes that the trained brain is physically different from the untrained one.

B The idea that we can train our brains to find more happiness has been called 'mindfulness' by neuropsychologist Rick Hanson, author of Hardwiring Happiness. It was in college that Hanson, quite unintentionally, first recognised the importance of something that would become his life's work. As an unconfident teenager, he discovered he could turn a small event, ‘a young woman smiling at me', into a good feeling he could hold on to. To do this, Hanson employs exactly the same imaginary 'video method' as psychiatrist Tony Fernando. ‘The brain takes its shape from what the mind rests upon,' says Hanson. If you keep resting your mind on self-criticism and worries, he argues, your brain will be shaped by that. Hanson explains that resting it on pleasant feelings and the things you have accomplished means that over time your brain will take on a different shape, with strength and optimism hard-wired into it.

C In New Zealand, the Mental Health Foundation runs mindfulness programmes in 14 schools. Foundation CEO Judi Clements says, 'It's a valuable approach because children are told to pay attention, but aren't told how to pay attention.' Preliminary results on the outcomes found that children had sustained increases in well-being. The Foundation recognises five pathways to happiness – being active, connecting with others, taking notice, learning and giving. And, says Clements, ‘We're detecting a hunger for it from different organisations and professions as well, so the Foundation is soon going to pilot an online “well-being game” in several workplaces.' The project leader is psychologist Carsten Grimm, who is interested in whether some pathways to happiness are more effective than others. In a study, Grimm recorded the activities and corresponding happiness scores of 173 people. What he found was that people who used several pathways to happiness achieved the best results, suggesting it's better to have a balance than concentrate on the single pathway you most identify with.

D However, Associate Professor of Psychological Medicine Nathan Consedine greets our relentless search for the secrets to happiness with a tired sigh. ‘The more you chase it, the less you get it,' he says, quoting studies showing those who value contentment and well-being are, in fact, less happy. The big question, he says, is whether there's any benefit in actively seeking happiness. He cites a study, for example, which showed that people who were happier were less inclined to show sympathy. Consedine says that's probably because happy people are strongly motivated to stay happy, but engaging sympathetically with others typically involves engaging with their distress, and that's going to reduce their own happiness. Consedine's not disagreeing with the theory of mindfulness, but believes there's more work to be done.

E Some of that work is being conducted at Auckland University's Centre for Brain Research. Associate Professor Johanna Montgomery has been studying Hanson's theory - that altering our brain activity at a synaptic level affects our behaviour. She accepts that it's a logical explanation based on studies from animals, but we haven't yet got the technology to prove it scientifically in humans. It's true that MRI scans certainly do indicate an increased flow of blood to different areas of the brain which are experiencing positive stimuli. However, she warns that this is a long way from confirming that the brain itself is developing or strengthening.

F Nonetheless, Montgomery believes she is making progress. In the laboratory, when scientists want to experiment with synaptic connections, they stimulate the brain with electricity, as this copies the high-frequency firings that happen normally in the brain every second. Using this technique, Montgomery has made a number of findings. For example, the hormones that are released routinely in response to good or bad situations – such as adrenaline – act to regulate the brain, in the same way that weather has a regulating effect on human activity more generally. But scientists understand some of these stimuli better than others. More is known about the impact on brain activity of prolonged periods of fear than the effects of ‘happiness' hormones that are released by positive events in life. This is one potentially important area that she hopes to investigate further in future.

questionGroups.bodyHtml:
Questions 14–17

Reading Passage 2 has six paragraphs, A–F.

Which paragraph contains the following information?

Write the correct letter, A–F, in boxes 14–17 on your answer sheet.

NB You may use any letter more than once.

ABCDEF
14 a reference to a fact that two scientists use the same technique to promote their own happiness
15 the suggestion that scientific opinion about an aspect of brain function has changed over a given time period
16 an estimate of how numerous some brain components are
17 the reason why some educational courses were set up

Questions 18–21

Look at the following statements (Questions 18–21) and the list of people below.

Match each statement with the correct person, A–F.

18 It's better to look for a variety of ways to increase happiness than focus on just one.

19 Focusing on personal achievements rather than negative experiences will make people happier.

20 Happy people might have a reason not to display one favourable characteristic.

21 A range of groups are becoming more interested in learning techniques to improve happiness.

List of People
A Tony Fernando
B Richard Davidson
C Rick Hanson
D Judi Clements
E Carsten Grimm
F Nathan Consedine

Questions 22–26

Complete the summary below.

Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.

Auckland University's Centre for Brain Research

Associate Professor Johanna Montgomery says that current research into brain activity and behaviour only relates to 22 so Hanson's theories have not been proved correct. While scans do show that positive stimuli result in more 23 reaching parts of the brain, this isn't proof that the brain is getting stronger.

But Montgomery is making progress. In laboratory experiments, scientists use 24 to initiate brain activity, because it's similar to natural processes. One finding is that hormones can be compared to the 25 because both can change human behaviour. But scientists understand some stimuli, such as 26 better than they understand more positive stimuli.

meta.title: How to be Happy 如何获得幸福

passageNotes.label: Paragraph A
passageNotes.text: 精神科医生Tony Fernando正走在街上，看到一群年轻的无家可归者坐在人行道上。当Fernando分发食物礼物时，他试图在脑海中录下这些人的反应，记录他们的感激之情如何反过来鼓舞了自己。他说：“我感到温暖、满足、有意义。”Fernando认为，大脑可以通过训练使我们快乐，而他的“录像法”就是实现这一目标的途径之一。事实上，国际上越来越多的科学研究表明，我们可以像学习弹钢琴一样学习获得幸福。在构成大脑的软组织中，大约有十万亿个突触连接着大约一千亿个神经元。活跃的突触变得更加敏感；不太活跃的突触会消亡，但新的突触会迅速生长。这是一种相对较新的认识——就在30年前，神经科学家还相信成年脑细胞无法再生。这一领域的先驱之一是威斯康星大学教授Richard Davidson。他在自己的研究设施中使用脑部扫描研究佛教僧侣，发现那些受过冥想训练的人左前额皮层（与幸福感相关的区域）的活动水平更高。Davidson相信，经过训练的大脑在生理上与未经训练的大脑是不同的。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph B
passageNotes.text: 神经心理学家Rick Hanson——《固化幸福》一书的作者——将我们可以训练大脑找到更多幸福这一理念称为“正念”。Hanson在大学时期无意中首次认识到某件事情的重要性，这件事后来成为了他毕生的事业。作为一个缺乏自信的青少年，他发现自己可以把一件小事——“一个年轻女子对我微笑”——转化为一种他可以保持的良好感觉。为了做到这一点，Hanson使用了与精神科医生Tony Fernando完全相同的想象“录像法”。Hanson说：“大脑的形状取决于心灵驻留在什么之上。”他认为，如果你一直让心灵停留在自我批评和担忧上，你的大脑就会被这些东西塑造。Hanson解释说，让心灵驻留在愉快的感觉和你所取得的成就上，意味着随着时间的推移，你的大脑会呈现出不同的形态，力量和乐观会固化其中。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph C
passageNotes.text: 在新西兰，心理健康基金会在14所学校开展正念课程。基金会首席执行官Judi Clements说：“这是一种有价值的方法，因为孩子们被告知要集中注意力，但没有人告诉他们如何集中注意力。”关于成果的初步调查结果显示，孩子们的幸福感持续提升。基金会确定了通往幸福的五条途径——保持活跃、与他人联系、留心观察、学习和给予。Clements说：“我们还发现来自不同组织和专业人士对此也有强烈的需求，因此基金会很快将在几个工作场所试点一个在线‘幸福游戏’。”该项目负责人是心理学家Carsten Grimm，他对某些幸福途径是否比其他途径更有效感兴趣。在一项研究中，Grimm记录了173人的活动及相应的幸福评分。他发现，使用多条幸福途径的人取得了最好的结果，这表明保持平衡比专注于你最认同的单一途径更好。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph D
passageNotes.text: 然而，心理医学副教授Nathan Consedine对我们不懈追寻幸福秘诀的做法报以一声疲惫的叹息。他说：“你越是追逐它，你得到的就越少。”他引用研究表明，那些重视满足感和幸福感的人实际上更不快乐。他说，一个重大问题是主动追求幸福是否有任何好处。他举例引用了一项研究，该研究表明更快乐的人不太倾向于表现出同情心。Consedine说，这可能是因为快乐的人有强烈的动力保持快乐，但富有同情心地与他人互动通常需要接触他人的痛苦，而这会降低他们自己的幸福感。Consedine并非不同意正念理论，但他认为还有更多工作要做。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph E
passageNotes.text: 其中一些工作正在奥克兰大学大脑研究中心进行。副教授Johanna Montgomery一直在研究Hanson的理论——即在突触层面改变我们的大脑活动会影响我们的行为。她承认这是基于动物研究得出的合理解释，但我们尚未拥有在人类身上进行科学验证的技术。确实，核磁共振扫描确实表明，在受到积极刺激时，流向大脑不同区域的血液增加了。然而，她警告说，这距离确认大脑本身正在发育或增强还有很长的路要走。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph F
passageNotes.text: 尽管如此，Montgomery相信她正在取得进展。在实验室中，当科学家们想要对突触连接进行实验时，他们用电流刺激大脑，因为这复制了大脑中每秒正常发生的高频放电。使用这种技术，Montgomery取得了一些发现。例如，应对好或坏情境时常规释放的激素——如肾上腺素——起到调节大脑的作用，就像天气对人类活动具有更广泛的调节效果一样。但科学家对其中一些刺激的了解比其他的更多。关于长时间恐惧对大脑活动影响的了解，多于对生活中积极事件释放的“幸福”激素影响的了解。这是她希望在未来进一步研究的一个潜在重要领域。

items.text:
（1）题目 14：a reference to a fact that two scientists use the same technique to promote their own happiness
题目翻译：提到两位科学家使用相同的方法来提升自己的幸福感。
答案：B
定位：正文 B 段，第4句
原文：To do this, Hanson employs exactly the same imaginary ‘video method’ as psychiatrist Tony Fernando.
译文：为做到这一点，Hanson 使用的正是与精神科医生 Tony Fernando 相同的想象式“视频方法”。

解析：exactly the same method 对应题干的 the same technique，两位科学家分别是 Hanson 与 Fernando，因此选 B。

（2）题目 15：the suggestion that scientific opinion about an aspect of brain function has changed over a given time period
题目翻译：暗示科学界对大脑功能某一方面的看法在一段时间内发生了变化。
答案：A
定位：正文 A 段，第8句
原文：This is relatively new thinking – just 30 years ago, neuroscientists believed that adult brain cells couldn’t regenerate.
译文：这是相对较新的观点——仅仅30年前，神经科学家还认为成年人的脑细胞不能再生。

解析：30 years ago 的旧观点与 relatively new thinking 形成时间对照，直接体现科学认识发生变化，因此选 A。

（3）题目 16：an estimate of how numerous some brain components are
题目翻译：对某些大脑组成部分数量的估计。
答案：A
定位：正文 A 段，第6句
原文：there are approximately ten trillion synapses connecting roughly a hundred billion neurons.
译文：大约有十万亿个突触连接着约一千亿个神经元。

解析：approximately 与 roughly 都表示估计，synapses 和 neurons 是大脑组成部分，因此选 A。

（4）题目 17：the reason why some educational courses were set up
题目翻译：开设某些教育课程的原因。
答案：C
定位：正文 C 段，第2句
原文：It’s a valuable approach because children are told to pay attention, but aren’t told how to pay attention.
译文：这种方法很有价值，因为孩子们被要求专注，却没有人告诉他们如何专注。

解析：because 后说明了学校开设正念课程的原因：孩子知道需要专注，却不知道具体方法，因此选 C。

items.text:
（1）题目 18：It’s better to look for a variety of ways to increase happiness than focus on just one.
题目翻译：与只专注一种方法相比，寻找多种提升幸福感的方法更好。
答案：E
定位：正文 C 段，末句
原文：people who used several pathways to happiness achieved the best results, suggesting it’s better to have a balance than concentrate on the single pathway you most identify with.
译文：使用多条幸福路径的人取得了最佳结果，这说明保持平衡比只专注于自己最认同的一条路径更好。

解析：several pathways 与 single pathway 构成题干所说的“多种方法”和“只专注一种”的对比；这是 Carsten Grimm 的研究，因此选 E。

（2）题目 19：Focusing on personal achievements rather than negative experiences will make people happier.
题目翻译：关注个人成就而不是负面经历，会让人更幸福。
答案：C
定位：正文 B 段，末两句
原文：resting it on pleasant feelings and the things you have accomplished means that over time your brain will take on a different shape, with strength and optimism hard-wired into it.
译文：把注意力放在愉快感受和已经取得的成就上，久而久之会使大脑形成不同状态，把力量和乐观固定下来。

解析：things you have accomplished 对应个人成就，前文的 self-criticism and worries 对应负面经历；这一观点来自 Rick Hanson，因此选 C。

（3）题目 20：Happy people might have a reason not to display one favourable characteristic.
题目翻译：幸福的人可能出于某种原因，不愿表现出一种良好品质。
答案：F
定位：正文 D 段，第4至5句
原文：people who were happier were less inclined to show sympathy. Consedine says that’s probably because happy people are strongly motivated to stay happy
译文：更幸福的人不太愿意表现同情；Consedine 认为，这可能是因为幸福的人强烈希望维持自己的幸福状态。

解析：favourable characteristic 指 sympathy，原文同时给出不愿表现同情的原因；该观点来自 Nathan Consedine，因此选 F。

（4）题目 21：A range of groups are becoming more interested in learning techniques to improve happiness.
题目翻译：越来越多不同群体开始对学习提升幸福感的技巧感兴趣。
答案：D
定位：正文 C 段，第5句
原文：We’re detecting a hunger for it from different organisations and professions as well
译文：我们还发现，不同组织和职业群体对此有强烈需求。

解析：different organisations and professions 对应各种群体，a hunger for it 对应兴趣和需求上升；说话者是 Judi Clements，因此选 D。

items.text:
（1）题目 22：Associate Professor Johanna Montgomery says that current research into brain activity and behaviour only relates to ________, so Hanson’s theories have not been proved correct. While scans do show that positive stimuli result in more ________ reaching parts of the brain, this isn’t proof that the brain is getting stronger. But Montgomery is making progress. In laboratory experiments, scientists use ________ to initiate brain activity, because it’s similar to natural processes. One finding is that hormones can be compared to the ________, because both can change human behaviour. But scientists understand some stimuli, such as ________, better than they understand more positive stimuli.
题目翻译：目前关于大脑活动与行为的研究只涉及________。
答案：animals
定位：正文 E 段，第2句
原文：She accepts that it’s a logical explanation based on studies from animals, but we haven’t yet got the technology to prove it scientifically in humans.
译文：她承认这是一种基于动物研究的合理解释，但我们尚无技术在人类身上进行科学验证。

解析：题干的 only relates to 与原文 studies from animals 对应；空格需要研究对象的核心名词 animals。

（2）题目 23：Associate Professor Johanna Montgomery says that current research into brain activity and behaviour only relates to ________, so Hanson’s theories have not been proved correct. While scans do show that positive stimuli result in more ________ reaching parts of the brain, this isn’t proof that the brain is getting stronger. But Montgomery is making progress. In laboratory experiments, scientists use ________ to initiate brain activity, because it’s similar to natural processes. One finding is that hormones can be compared to the ________, because both can change human behaviour. But scientists understand some stimuli, such as ________, better than they understand more positive stimuli.
题目翻译：积极刺激会使更多________到达大脑的不同区域。
答案：blood
定位：正文 E 段，第3句
原文：MRI scans certainly do indicate an increased flow of blood to different areas of the brain which are experiencing positive stimuli.
译文：核磁共振扫描确实显示，受到积极刺激的大脑不同区域会有更多血液流入。

解析：题干已有 more 和 reaching，原文中真正到达大脑各区域的是 blood，因此填 blood。

（3）题目 24：Associate Professor Johanna Montgomery says that current research into brain activity and behaviour only relates to ________, so Hanson’s theories have not been proved correct. While scans do show that positive stimuli result in more ________ reaching parts of the brain, this isn’t proof that the brain is getting stronger. But Montgomery is making progress. In laboratory experiments, scientists use ________ to initiate brain activity, because it’s similar to natural processes. One finding is that hormones can be compared to the ________, because both can change human behaviour. But scientists understand some stimuli, such as ________, better than they understand more positive stimuli.
题目翻译：科学家使用________来启动大脑活动。
答案：electricity
定位：正文 F 段，第2句
原文：they stimulate the brain with electricity, as this copies the high-frequency firings that happen normally in the brain every second.
译文：他们用电刺激大脑，因为这会模拟大脑每秒自然发生的高频放电。

解析：use ... to initiate brain activity 对应 stimulate the brain with electricity，因此填 electricity。

（4）题目 25：Associate Professor Johanna Montgomery says that current research into brain activity and behaviour only relates to ________, so Hanson’s theories have not been proved correct. While scans do show that positive stimuli result in more ________ reaching parts of the brain, this isn’t proof that the brain is getting stronger. But Montgomery is making progress. In laboratory experiments, scientists use ________ to initiate brain activity, because it’s similar to natural processes. One finding is that hormones can be compared to the ________, because both can change human behaviour. But scientists understand some stimuli, such as ________, better than they understand more positive stimuli.
题目翻译：激素可以与________相比，因为二者都能改变人的行为。
答案：weather
定位：正文 F 段，第4句
原文：the hormones that are released routinely in response to good or bad situations – such as adrenaline – act to regulate the brain, in the same way that weather has a regulating effect on human activity more generally.
译文：日常因好坏情境释放的激素会调节大脑，就像天气对人的活动具有调节作用一样。

解析：题干的 can be compared to 对应 in the same way that，比较对象是 weather，因此填 weather。

（5）题目 26：Associate Professor Johanna Montgomery says that current research into brain activity and behaviour only relates to ________, so Hanson’s theories have not been proved correct. While scans do show that positive stimuli result in more ________ reaching parts of the brain, this isn’t proof that the brain is getting stronger. But Montgomery is making progress. In laboratory experiments, scientists use ________ to initiate brain activity, because it’s similar to natural processes. One finding is that hormones can be compared to the ________, because both can change human behaviour. But scientists understand some stimuli, such as ________, better than they understand more positive stimuli.
题目翻译：科学家对某些刺激（例如________）的了解，多于对积极刺激的了解。
答案：fear
定位：正文 F 段，第6句
原文：More is known about the impact on brain activity of prolonged periods of fear than the effects of ‘happiness’ hormones that are released by positive events in life.
译文：人们对长期恐惧如何影响大脑活动的了解，多于对生活中积极事件释放的“幸福”激素作用的了解。

解析：More is known ... than 对应 understand ... better than；原文给出的负面刺激例子是 fear。
